implementation_design.arbitration: Independent display-DRAM and sprite-SRAM buses. Display reads and full-array refresh have bounded host/DMA backpressure. Sprite fetches use the separate SRAM bus and existing staging/shifters; completed FIFO banks preserve raster order.
implementation_design.text_fetch: Cache 80 character codes and 80 attributes; prefetch the next row into the second 160-byte cache over eight glyph scanlines. Expand each glyph byte to eight 4-bit pixels; prefetch sprite rows and apply fixed priority before publishing pixels.
implementation_design.line_repeat: Re-fetch repeated bitmap lines; FIFO capacity is not an additional framebuffer or guaranteed retained scanline. Validate 320x100x4 bandwidth and refresh at the selected DRAM grade.

clock_targets.scope: 14.31818 MHz short scanout/counter path; renderer uses block expansion and clock enables, not a full CPU at pixel rate. Process-corner qualification required.

manufacturing_planning.process: 3–3.5 micron NMOS; laser-written process-matched masks from secret facility; wafer fabrication at AION Labs.
external_functions: Two AION 2114-equivalent SRAM chips on a separate sprite bus; enlarged interface package/PCB allowance costed at assembly level

engines.renderer: Dedicated fetch/address, eight-pixel glyph expansion, colour selection and fixed-priority sprite compositor; not a general-purpose CPU. Runs when a free FIFO bank and source data are available.
engines.scanout: Independent fixed-raster sequencer reads completed 4-bit pixels and generates sync. Both engines use the same master clock with clock enables.
engines.fifo: Four 40-byte addressed banks with output latches; ordered circular FREE/FILLING/READY/READING ownership. Publish complete banks only; backpressure on full FIFO; prefill before active display.
engines.underrun: Continue sync, emit border colour and latch diagnostic status; never read a partially rendered bank.

timing_budget.qualification: 100 display-DRAM reads average 37.5 us; 40 sprite bytes take 10 us on a separate bus. Descriptor reads and row transitions also need scheduling. Prove local FIFO deadlines, refresh, repeated bitmap lines and uploads; these averages are not a timing proof.

implementation_design.sprite_access: Two AION 2114-equivalent chips form an exclusive 1 KiB 8-bit SRAM bank. Auto-increment upload ports arbitrate CPU/DMA writes against sprite reads; descriptor-bank selection latches at vertical blank.

pixel_buffer.policy: FREE/FILLING/READY/READING banks; output latches and serializer. Never overwrite active bank; underrun preserves sync.

chapters.description:
This dedicated graphics ASIC produces {pixel_bits}-bit pixel indices. It performs fetch/address generation, eight-pixel glyph expansion, colour selection and fixed-priority sprite composition; it is not a general-purpose CPU. A separately clock-enabled raster sequencer consumes completed pixels and generates sync.

External display RAM is {display_ram_kib} KiB from {display_chip_count} {display_chip_id} chips. Two {sprite_chip_id} devices form a separate 1 KiB, 8-bit sprite bank. Auto-increment uploads arbitrate against sprite reads; descriptor-bank selection latches at vertical blank. Display reads and full-array refresh impose bounded host/DMA backpressure.

The on-chip storage budget is {internal_storage_bytes} bytes, included in die estimates: two 160-byte character/attribute row caches, 40-byte sprite shifters, 40-byte sprite staging and a four-bank, 160-byte pixel FIFO. Each 40-byte FIFO bank holds 4-bit pixels and moves through {fifo_states}; publish complete banks only, backpressure a full queue and prefill before active display. Underrun emits border colour, maintains sync and records diagnostic status.

The text engine caches eighty character codes and attributes and prefetches the next row over eight glyph scanlines. It expands each glyph byte into eight pixels, fetches sprite rows and applies priority before publishing. Repeated bitmap lines are fetched again: the FIFO is neither an extra framebuffer nor a guaranteed retained scanline.

The master and high-resolution pixel clock target {master_clock_mhz} MHz; low-resolution scanout targets {low_resolution_clock_mhz} MHz. The maximum FIFO output target is {fifo_output_mbytes_s} Mbytes/s. Only short scanout/counter paths operate at dot rate; renderer work uses block expansion and clock enables.

At the 375 ns DRAM-cycle target, eighty glyph reads plus twenty amortized next-row bytes give one hundred display reads and 37.5 µs per scanline on average. Forty sprite bytes take 10 µs on their independent bus at a 250 ns SRAM cycle. The full FIFO holds 320 pixels and drains in 22.349 µs at high resolution; two ready pages allow 11.175 µs. Row transitions, descriptors, refresh, repeated bitmap lines and uploads still require deadline analysis and process-corner qualification; these averages are not a timing proof.

The manufacturing plan uses 3–3.5 µm NMOS, process-matched laser-written masks from the secret facility and AION Labs wafer fabrication. Estimated transistor count is {transistor_range}, with {central_transistor_count} as the central value. At 3 µm, die area is estimated at {die_area_3um_range_mm2} mm², central {die_area_3um_central_mm2}; at 3.5 µm it is {die_area_3_5um_range_mm2} mm², central {die_area_3_5um_central_mm2}.

Display DRAM, sprite SRAM, cable drivers/transceivers and monitor palette/DAC circuitry remain external. The larger sprite-interface package and PCB allowance belongs to assembly cost, not additional on-chip storage.

specification.mode_discovery: Enumerate controller modes intersected with identified or configured monitor raster capabilities and available buffering/sprite allocations. Reject unsupported downscaling.

memory_layout.mode_exclusivity: Text/font and bitmap allocations are alternative uses of 32 KiB display DRAM. Exclusive 1 KiB sprite SRAM is available in every mode.
memory_layout.font_policy: One shared 256-glyph bank per mode. Font allocation 2048 bytes at 8×8, 4096 at 8×16 or 8×10 (16-byte glyph stride). Font writes affect both pages.
memory_layout.page_flip: Latch selected page during vertical blank; drawing throughput is not guaranteed by double buffering.

sprites.coordinate_space: Logical mode pixels; scale together with the background. Signed 16-bit X and Y; clip at screen edges.
sprites.priority: Lower sprite number wins; all sprites overlay background/text.
sprites.registers: Two descriptor banks hold signed 16-bit X/Y, enable and reserved controls. CPU/DMA uses auto-incrementing SRAM upload ports.
sprites.allocation_policy: Five sprites in every text/bitmap mode, including double-buffered backgrounds. Sprite SRAM never consumes display DRAM.
sprites.descriptor_allocation_note: 80 bytes of live two-bank descriptors within a 128-byte reserved area; 48 bytes padding. 640 pattern + 128 descriptor + 256 scratch bytes = 1024.

display_memory.organization: 16K × 16 bits; ordinary external DRAM, independent display refresh sequencer.

pixel_buffer.location: On video ASIC; SRAM banks with page ownership latches
pixel_buffer.policy: Eight-pixel parallel renderer fills free pages; independent clocked serializer drains ready pages. Two pages per 640-pixel line; prefill before active display; never overwrite displaying pages. Underflow blanks pixels, preserves sync and sets sticky fault.
pixel_buffer.physical_organization: Each 160-byte bank is 40 words × 32 bits. Load eight 4-bit pixels into a separate 32-bit serializer latch every eight dot clocks, then shift at 21.504 MHz. SRAM array reads run at 2.688 MHz, not one read per dot; filler and drain use different banks.

character_row_cache.purpose: Current and next 80-column character/attribute row; separate from 640-byte pixel FIFO.

timing_budget.qualification: At 250 ns conservative DRAM cycle, 80 glyph fetches consume 20 microseconds per active line; 160-byte row prefetch amortizes across 8/10/16 scanlines. Two row caches and 16-bit reads cover text-row transitions. Verify sprites, refresh and bounded host/DMA slots together at voltage/temperature corners; no guaranteed maximum CPU upload rate.

specification.arbitration: Card-local sequencer arbitrates display fetch and deadline-reserved independent DRAM refresh before bounded host/DMA transfers with READY. Sprite SRAM has its own 8-bit bus. System DMA/MMU remain dedicated host components; the card does not replace system-memory refresh.
specification.monitor_policy: Read capability descriptor before enabling sync. Mono Pro accepts only raster_640_400; integer-scale legacy modes. Old monitors retain their advertised 200-line raster(s), never 640×400. Native 400-line modes require Mono Pro; new 200-line bitmap modes also work on capable older displays. This is display-mode/API compatibility, not Z80 binary compatibility.

requirements.description: External 16×4116 DRAM and 2×2114 sprite SRAM; integrated 640-byte pixel FIFO and 320-byte row cache. Die-area estimate 80 mm² (60–110), about 65,000–95,000 transistors including SRAM; not a released layout. Qualify timing, large-package pin count, analog-free digital logic and one respin.

chapters.description:
The controller implements {video_link_id} through {display_api_id}. Software selects only modes supported by the controller, monitor profile and available buffer/sprite allocation; unsupported downscaling is rejected.

The corresponding board is {card_id}; external RAM populations below describe that board rather than memory integrated on the die. The controller has a planning die area of {die_area_mm2} mm², not a measured production die.

Display storage is {video_ram_kib} KiB, built from {display_chip_count} {display_chip_id} devices on a {display_bus_bits}-bit bus. Text/font and bitmap allocations are alternative uses of this memory. Sprite storage is independent: {sprite_ram_bytes} bytes from {sprite_chip_count} {sprite_chip_id} chips on a separate {sprite_bus_bits}-bit bus.

One shared 256-glyph bank per mode. Font allocation 2048 bytes at 8×8, 4096 at 8×16 or 8×10 (16-byte glyph stride). Font writes affect both pages.

Page selection latches during vertical blank. Double buffering does not guarantee drawing throughput.

The ASIC pixel pipeline contains {pixel_buffer_pages} banks of {pixel_buffer_page_bytes} bytes, holding {pixel_depth_bits}-bit pixels. Separate ownership states prevent the renderer from overwriting a bank being scanned out: {pixel_bank_states}. Completed banks feed output latches and a serializer; the pipeline is prefetched before active display and preserves sync on underrun.

Each bank comprises 40 × 32-bit words and holds 320 pixels, so a 640-pixel line consumes two banks. The renderer expands eight pixels at a time while a separate serializer latch drains ready banks. Underrun blanks pixels and sets a sticky fault.

Two {character_cache_bytes}-byte row caches hold current and next character/attribute rows independently of the pixel FIFO.

The dot clock is {pixel_clock_mhz} MHz. Eight-pixel renderer steps and SRAM latch loads run at {renderer_step_mhz} MHz, rather than requiring one SRAM read per dot. A pixel bank drains in {pixel_bank_drain_us} µs.

Card-local sequencer arbitrates display fetch and deadline-reserved independent DRAM refresh before bounded host/DMA transfers with READY. Sprite SRAM has its own 8-bit bus. System DMA/MMU remain dedicated host components; the card does not replace system-memory refresh.

At 250 ns conservative DRAM cycle, 80 glyph fetches consume 20 microseconds per active line; 160-byte row prefetch amortizes across 8/10/16 scanlines. Two row caches and 16-bit reads cover text-row transitions. Verify sprites, refresh and bounded host/DMA slots together at voltage/temperature corners; no guaranteed maximum CPU upload rate.

Read capability descriptor before enabling sync. Mono Pro accepts only raster_640_400; integer-scale legacy modes. Old monitors retain their advertised 200-line raster(s), never 640×400. Native 400-line modes require Mono Pro; new 200-line bitmap modes also work on capable older displays. This is display-mode/API compatibility, not Z80 binary compatibility.

Up to {sprite_count} sprites can appear on each scanline. Each is {sprite_size} pixels at {sprite_bits_per_pixel} bits per pixel, with index {transparent_index} transparent. Lower sprite numbers take priority over higher ones, and all overlay text or background. Signed 16-bit logical coordinates scale with the background and clip at screen edges.

Five patterns occupy 640 bytes. Two banks of 8-byte descriptors use 80 live bytes within a 128-byte reservation, leaving 48 bytes of padding and 256 bytes of scratch space in sprite SRAM. Auto-increment upload ports accept CPU/DMA transfers. Descriptors are banked; patterns are not double-buffered. All sprites remain available when the background is double-buffered.

specification.mode_discovery: Enumerate controller modes intersected with identified or configured monitor raster capabilities and available buffering/sprite allocations. Reject unsupported downscaling.

memory_layout.mode_exclusivity: Text/font and bitmap allocations are alternative uses of 32 KiB display DRAM. Exclusive 1 KiB sprite SRAM is available in every mode.
memory_layout.font_policy: One shared 256-glyph bank per mode. Font allocation 2048 bytes at 8×8, 4096 at 8×16 or 8×10 (16-byte glyph stride). Font writes affect both pages.
memory_layout.page_flip: Latch selected page during vertical blank; drawing throughput is not guaranteed by double buffering.

sprites.coordinate_space: Logical mode pixels; scale together with the background. Signed 16-bit X and Y; clip at screen edges.
sprites.priority: Lower sprite number wins; all sprites overlay background/text.
sprites.registers: Two descriptor banks hold signed 16-bit X/Y, enable and reserved controls. CPU/DMA uses auto-incrementing SRAM upload ports.
sprites.allocation_policy: Five sprites in every text/bitmap mode, including double-buffered backgrounds. Sprite SRAM never consumes display DRAM.
sprites.descriptor_allocation_note: 80 bytes of live two-bank descriptors within a 128-byte reserved area; 48 bytes padding. 640 pattern + 128 descriptor + 256 scratch bytes = 1024.

display_memory.organization: 16K × 16 bits; ordinary external DRAM, independent display refresh sequencer.

pixel_buffer.location: On video ASIC; SRAM banks with page ownership latches
pixel_buffer.policy: Eight-pixel parallel renderer fills free pages; independent clocked serializer drains ready pages. Two pages per 640-pixel line; prefill before active display; never overwrite displaying pages. Underflow blanks pixels, preserves sync and sets sticky fault.
pixel_buffer.physical_organization: Each 160-byte bank is 40 words × 32 bits. Load eight 4-bit pixels into a separate 32-bit serializer latch every eight dot clocks, then shift at 21.504 MHz. SRAM array reads run at 2.688 MHz, not one read per dot; filler and drain use different banks.

character_row_cache.purpose: Current and next 80-column character/attribute row; separate from 640-byte pixel FIFO.

timing_budget.qualification: At 250 ns conservative DRAM cycle, 80 glyph fetches consume 20 microseconds per active line; 160-byte row prefetch amortizes across 8/10/16 scanlines. Two row caches and 16-bit reads cover text-row transitions. Verify sprites, refresh and bounded host/DMA slots together at voltage/temperature corners; no guaranteed maximum CPU upload rate.

specification.arbitration: Card-local sequencer arbitrates display fetch and deadline-reserved independent DRAM refresh before bounded host/DMA transfers with READY. Sprite SRAM has its own 8-bit bus. System DMA/MMU remain dedicated host components; the card does not replace system-memory refresh.

This is display-mode/API compatibility, not Z80 binary compatibility.

Display storage is {video_ram_kib} KiB, built from {display_chip_count} {display_chip_id} devices on a {display_bus_bits}-bit bus. Text/font and bitmap allocations are alternative uses of this memory. Sprite storage is independent: {sprite_ram_bytes} bytes from {sprite_chip_count} {sprite_chip_id} chips on a separate {sprite_bus_bits}-bit bus.

Page selection latches during vertical blank. Double buffering does not guarantee drawing throughput.

The ASIC pixel pipeline contains {pixel_buffer_pages} banks of {pixel_buffer_page_bytes} bytes, holding {pixel_depth_bits}-bit pixels. Separate ownership states prevent the renderer from overwriting a bank being scanned out: {pixel_bank_states}. Completed banks feed output latches and a serializer; the pipeline is prefetched before active display and preserves sync on underrun.

dma.bank_selection: Latch physical source/destination bank and offsets on start. CPU mapping changes cannot redirect an active transfer; split logical buffers at 4 KiB boundaries before programming physical segments. Reject ROM writes, unmapped banks and out-of-range lengths.
dma.arbitration: Bounded bursts with guaranteed CPU and refresh service; device-ready/WAIT handshake; video uploads yield to video-controller fetch deadlines. Numeric grant limits require cycle-level validation.
dma.completion: Completion/error interrupt, readable remaining count, controlled abort; reset disables DMA.
dma.video_endpoint: Auto-incrementing upload ports for display DRAM or dedicated sprite SRAM; target-ready backpressure.
dma.peripheral_scope: Disk/FlexiBUS DMA requires qualified request/ready or FIFO endpoints and drivers; legacy programmed I/O remains supported.

refresh.scope: System DRAM only, including hidden banks and expansion. Video controller refreshes display DRAM; sprite SRAM needs no refresh.

chapters.description:
This controller serves {host_clocks_mhz} MHz Aurelia hosts with a {address_bits}-bit CPU address interface and an {data_bits}-bit data bus. The map fixes lower RAM at 0000–6FFF, switches 4 KiB pages in 7000–EFFF and preserves common RAM at F000–FFFF; boot ROM appears at zero until normal-map release.

An always-running refresh timer, row counter and arbiter operate during execution, HALT and DMA. Initialize them before using RAM and qualify row count/retention against the installed chips. Supported system populations are {supported_populations}. Hidden pages and expansion RAM are included; display RAM is refreshed by the video controller, while sprite SRAM needs none.

The controller has {dma_contexts} transfer contexts and {dma_engines} active engine, with 16-bit destination addresses and lengths. Supported operations are {dma_operations} with {address_steps} addressing. Physical source/destination banks and offsets latch at start; split logical buffers at page boundaries, and reject ROM writes, unmapped banks and invalid lengths.

Bounded bursts preserve CPU and refresh service and honour device-ready/WAIT handshakes; video uploads yield to display deadlines. Completion/error interrupts, a readable remaining count and controlled abort expose transfer state; reset disables DMA. Display and sprite uploads use auto-increment ports with backpressure. Disk/FlexiBUS DMA needs qualified request/ready or FIFO endpoints and drivers, while programmed I/O remains supported. Numeric grant limits need cycle-level validation.

specification.continuity: Retain prior modes, five sprites with independent SRAM, pixel FIFO, character caches, refresh and host/DMA arbitration. Canonical detailed layout resides in the card specification.

pixel_buffer.location: On video ASIC; SRAM banks with page ownership latches
pixel_buffer.policy: Eight-pixel parallel renderer fills free pages; independent clocked serializer drains ready pages. Two pages per 640-pixel line; prefill before active display; never overwrite displaying pages. Underflow blanks pixels, preserves sync and sets sticky fault.
pixel_buffer.physical_organization: Each 160-byte bank is 40 words × 32 bits. Load eight 4-bit pixels into a separate 32-bit serializer latch every eight dot clocks, then shift at 21.504 MHz. SRAM array reads run at 2.688 MHz, not one read per dot; filler and drain use different banks.

character_row_cache.purpose: Current and next 80-column character/attribute row; separate from 640-byte pixel FIFO.

requirements.description: Functional-set procurement allowance; detailed supplier selection pending.
Engineering baseline; electrical qualification, routing and supplier quotes pending.

chapters.description: This revision extends {base_controller_id} for {card_id}. It adds 64 KiB display addressing, 640 × 400 × 2bpp and 640 × 200 × 4bpp modes, and bounded prefetch/sequencing for {palette_list_id}. Earlier modes, five sprites with independent SRAM, refresh and bounded host/DMA arbitration remain part of the design.

The ASIC pixel pipeline contains {pixel_buffer_pages} banks of {pixel_buffer_page_bytes} bytes, holding {pixel_depth_bits}-bit pixels. Separate ownership states prevent the renderer from overwriting a bank being scanned out: {pixel_bank_states}. Completed banks feed output latches and a serializer; the pipeline is prefetched before active display and preserves sync on underrun.

Each bank comprises 40 × 32-bit words and holds 320 pixels, so a 640-pixel line consumes two banks. The renderer expands eight pixels at a time while a separate serializer latch drains ready banks. Underrun blanks pixels and sets a sticky fault.

Two {character_cache_bytes}-byte row caches hold current and next character/attribute rows independently of the pixel FIFO.

The serializer shifts at 21.504 MHz, loading eight pixels every eight dot clocks; SRAM latch reads therefore run at 2.688 MHz with filler and drain on different banks.

reporting.continuity: Extend Abacus 2.0 report/document layouts, spreadsheet fields and one-off/repeating sections.
reporting.presentation: Retain standard TUI editing/navigation; add capability-aware graphical preview with titles, axes and legends. Support monochrome patterns and available display modes through the display API.
reporting.output: Print reports and charts through supported printer drivers; define pagination and refresh stale query/formula results before output.

data_interchange.bpi_continuity: Retain versioned BPI summary imports as independent planning inputs with reconciliation and decimal validation; no ledger write-back or live database connection.
data_interchange.csv: Schema-mapped CSV import with quoted fields, delimiter/character encoding selection, explicit date and decimal conventions, null handling, text preservation for identifiers and rejected-record diagnostics. data_interchange.vsam: Import host-exported sequential logical records from supported VSAM datasets using a supplied field/record layout. Host-side export (for example IDCAMS REPRO) and a documented transfer path are prerequisites; raw VSAM clusters, indexes and disk images are not desktop interchange formats.
data_interchange.vsam_conversion: Declare supported record boundaries, lengths, offsets, keys and character encoding; convert EBCDIC, supported binary, packed-decimal and zoned-decimal fields explicitly. Reject unsupported layouts without silently changing values.
data_interchange.migration: Versioned document format; preserve supported older worksheets and reports. Older Abacus/Pulse editions must reject unsupported new features before writing. Explicit value-only export is a lossy interchange option.

release_scope.launch: Flat typed formatted tables, bounded columnar processing, virtual columns, unique-key lookups, a documented read-only SQL subset, graphical reports, embedded Pulse and mapped imports.
later_milestones: Bounded nested arrays, maps and structs with explicit expansion/indexing and aggregation semantics; format extension points reserved in 3.0.
Broader query capabilities and competitive response to Lotus 1-2-3 in a later Abacus version.
release_scope.resource_policy: Qualify real Artemis 128/256 KiB configurations and later Artemis PRO separately. Record application/OS memory, storage, dataset size and timings; larger jobs may require expansion or disk-backed execution. No new minimum RAM or maximum row count is asserted.
release_scope.acceptance_workflow: Import sales records, join customer/product information, calculate margins, group by region, print a graphical report, save/reopen, then repeat using a Pulse script.
acceptance_requirements: Measure memory, disk I/O, import/query/recalculation/report times and compression on named datasets.
Verify import conversion/rejections, decimal rounding, nulls, duplicate lookup keys and join cardinality.
Verify cancellation, grouped undo, edit visibility, dependency invalidation, save recovery and unsupported-version rejection.

chapters.description:
Abacus 3 is the native 32-bit Artemis spreadsheet and analysis line. Sparse worksheets and schema-defined formatted-table tabs coexist with multiple tabs, cross-tab references, typed columns, virtual calculated columns, unique-key lookups and a documented read-only SQL subset. Disk-backed columnar storage uses column pruning, conservative statistics-based skipping and dataset-dependent encoding rather than promised compression or throughput.

Reports extend earlier spreadsheet-field layouts with one-off/repeating sections and graphical {chart_types} charts. Capability-aware preview includes titles, axes and legends while retaining standard TUI editing and monochrome patterns. Supported printer drivers paginate output; refresh stale query/formula results before printing.

Embedded Pulse uses the Abacus-owned document API; standalone Pulse retains exclusive offline access to supported closed files. Preserve formulas and invalidate changed cached results rather than allowing a second concurrent writer.

Versioned BPI summaries remain independent planning inputs with decimal checks and reconciliation, without ledger write-back or a live database link. CSV import maps schemas, quoting, delimiters, encodings, dates, decimal conventions, nulls and text identifiers, with rejected-record diagnostics. Value-only export explicitly loses formulas and types.

VSAM import consumes host-exported sequential logical records, for example through IDCAMS REPRO, with a supplied record layout and transfer path. Declare boundaries, lengths, offsets and keys; convert EBCDIC, supported binary, packed decimal and zoned decimal explicitly. Raw VSAM images, clusters and indexes are not desktop interchange files. Reject unsupported layouts without reinterpretation. Preserve older document versions; older Abacus/Pulse editions must reject unsupported new features before writing.

The initial release uses flat formatted tables. Bounded nested arrays/maps/structs with explicit aggregation/expansion and broader Lotus 1-2-3 response features are later work. It does not promise background recalculation, unlimited documents/memory, a full transactional SQL database, arbitrary VSAM image access or unrestricted nested data.

Qualify actual Artemis 128/256 KiB and later PRO configurations separately. Measure memory, storage, timing, I/O and compression on named datasets; larger jobs may need expansion or disk-backed processing. Exercise sales import, customer/product joins, margins, regional grouping, printed charts, save/reopen and the equivalent Pulse script. Check conversions, rounding, nulls, duplicate keys, join cardinality, cancellation, grouped undo, visibility, dependency invalidation, recovery and unsupported-version rejection. No unmeasured minimum RAM or maximum row count is asserted.

The implementation uses {portable_api_id}. Keep application/document algorithms separate from platform adapters; query display dimensions and attributes, use semantic colours and clipping, and handle allocation failures with bounded buffers and banked-object handles. Persistent records are explicitly encoded and versioned rather than raw structures or pointers. Recompile and adapt OS-specific modules for another target, then test its resource limits; source portability does not extend the list of qualified hosts.

This application suite targets native ERA/AIONix on {host_base_computer_artemis} and {host_base_computer_artemis_pro}. It requires {runtime_aionix_os_model}. The edition is delivered on diskette. Application workspace and ROM footprint remain unspecified.

abacus_file_integration.model: Read/edit/write Abacus document files; not live application integration.

abacus_file_integration.format_policy: Check format version and supported features before writing; reject unsupported edits without silently dropping data.
abacus_file_integration.save_policy: Write a replacement file, validate it, then perform a recoverable replacement retaining the prior version until success.
abacus_file_integration.formula_policy: Preserve formula text/encoding. Mark cached results invalid after edits; Abacus recalculates on opening unless Pulse has the matching evaluation library.
abacus_file_integration.memory_policy: Bounded record/cell iteration; whole-document duplication in RAM is not required.
abacus_file_integration.cross_version_policy: Each edition declares supported document-format versions. Later Artemis features are not implicitly writable by the Z80 edition.

chapters.description:
AIONix2 develops {baseline_os_id} for {processor_architecture_id}, retaining {portable_api_id}. The initial release combines executable system ROM, documented legacy ABI compatibility, protected preemptive user processes, recoverable HDD storage, users/permissions, a POSIX-oriented subset and an event-driven TUI foundation.

ROM execution/ABI, resilient multitasking and recoverable storage are essential, followed by access enforcement and the staged interface/UI work. Paging, metadata journaling, broader networking, threads/locales and a full windowed GUI remain later work, not initial release gates. These are engineering priorities rather than completed qualification.

Stable kernel code, core libraries, a small shell/basic utilities and recovery tools share read-only, cacheable executable ROM; each process keeps writable state in DRAM. The replaceable system cartridge supplies at least {minimum_os_rom_bytes} bytes. EEPROM BIOS remains boot/diagnostic firmware; optional services, larger utilities and patches load from disk rather than copying the entire ROM into RAM.

Executable ABI versions select legacy adapters, stable library dispatch and capability discovery. Preserve documented ERA instruction semantics, C calling conventions and layouts, syscall entry/numbers, loading, errors and legacy signals. Privileged drivers, undocumented kernel assumptions and direct hardware access need separate qualification; Z80 C code must be recompiled. Versioned dispatch and page-sized RAM overlays patch code after ROM checksum/version checks, with recovery boot bypassing disk patches. A qualified minor revision can be installed by exchanging a host-compatible cartridge.

The preferred DRAM allocation is {preferred_dram_bytes} bytes; the 256 KiB minimum is an engineering fit target, not a measured guarantee, and the server retains its existing 1 MiB configuration. Illustrative allocations are 40 KiB for kernel state/tables/stacks, 24 KiB for filesystem buffers, 16 KiB for translation metadata, 12 KiB for terminal/UI input, 20 KiB for services/patch reserve and 144 KiB for applications. Shared ROM, sparse page tables, small kernel stacks and reliable copy-on-write reduce demand. Allocation failure must be handled; ROM cannot replace writable RAM. Later swap requires qualified restart, locking and I/O with fault handlers resident, and should address occasional pressure rather than routine oversizing.

A compact monolithic kernel timer-preempts user processes while bounding non-preemptible kernel critical sections. Priority aging, sleeping I/O and atomic sleep/wakeup provide fairness; short interrupts defer work. Validate user pointers, protect kernel/device mappings, constrain per-process memory/files/requests, bound driver retries and timeouts, and retain responsive administrative termination. Process exit cleans files, memory, locks and child state. Kernel-controlled DMA uses checked pinned buffers; process isolation alone protects neither kernel/driver faults nor DMA. A fully preemptible kernel and application threads are not initial requirements.

A versioned inode filesystem separates directory entries from metadata, using {allocation_block_bytes}-byte blocks and {block_identifier_bits}-bit block IDs. The initial qualification range is {qualification_volume_mb} MB, not a capacity ceiling or bundled-drive change. Direct/indirect pointers, metadata timestamps/link counts, bounded caches, mounts and logical-sector drivers with CHS translation support the layout.

Clean/dirty state, a consistency checker, ordered metadata writes, explicit synchronization and tested backup/restore establish recoverability. Exact disk format/limits, file-offset and timestamp representation, legacy import/mount behaviour and controller persistence guarantees remain open. A later small metadata journal still needs power-loss/write-order testing and does not alone ensure application-data durability.

Numeric users/groups, owner/group/other permissions including directory search, creation masks, real/effective credentials and login/home directories define access. Protect salted, costed password hashes within CPU budgets and enforce permissions on every relevant kernel operation. Device/mount/configuration administration and audit records are protected. Qualify credential/exec transitions before enabling set-user-ID programs; servers authenticate users rather than trusting supplied UIDs. Extended ACLs are later work.

The initial subset defines file/descriptor operations and errors; descriptor duplication/inheritance; copy-on-write fork, exec, wait, status and environment; signals/masks/dispositions and interruption; canonical/raw terminals and foreground process groups; hierarchical paths, working directories and hard/symbolic links; pipes, EOF/broken-pipe handling and readiness multiplexing; shell quoting, redirection, pipelines, variables and statuses; wall and monotonic clocks with explicit timestamp formats. Publish an implemented/partial/absent matrix and unsupported-operation errors rather than claiming conformance from names. Efficient spawn, broader file control/mapping, full job control/pseudo-terminals, sockets/IPC, utilities, locales, threads and timers are later additions.

Applications own business logic and semantic Open/Save/Select/Cancel commands. A shared abstraction provides events, menus, forms, lists, focus, layout, measurement and drawing contexts; translation adapters preserve TUI, terminal, device and legacy ABI behaviour above native process/file/IPC/timer/input/display services. These are logical library/service layers, not four mandatory processes or IPC hops.

A bounded event queue handles keys, timers, focus, redraw and future pointer events. Opaque view/window handles initially describe text regions; clipping, invalidation, repaint, layout constraints and text measurement use separate cell/pixel coordinates. Clipboard/selection ownership is bounded, and graphics/font/colour/pointer support is discovered by version and capability. Compact text state, dirty regions and redraw callbacks avoid a mandatory full-screen backing bitmap. A later GUI can host old character applications in terminal windows without automatically redesigning them.

Release tests must cover legacy binary regressions, fairness/termination under CPU load, injected faults and cleanup, concurrent disk/terminal/DMA I/O, power loss and durable saves, credentials/permissions, measured ROM/RAM use with Abacus/compiler/server workloads, and TUI fallback/legacy terminal behaviour.

The software image is supplied in its matching physical ROM cartridge; hardware construction belongs to that cartridge. Application workspace and ROM footprint remain unspecified beyond the explicit system-ROM requirement.

chapters.description:
AIONix2 develops {baseline_os_id} for {processor_architecture_id}, retaining {portable_api_id}. The initial release combines executable system ROM, documented legacy ABI compatibility, protected preemptive user processes, recoverable HDD storage, users/permissions, a POSIX-oriented subset and an event-driven TUI foundation.

ROM execution/ABI, resilient multitasking and recoverable storage are essential, followed by access enforcement and the staged interface/UI work. Paging, metadata journaling, broader networking, threads/locales and a full windowed GUI remain later work, not initial release gates. These are engineering priorities rather than completed qualification.

Stable kernel code, core libraries, a small shell/basic utilities and recovery tools share read-only, cacheable executable ROM; each process keeps writable state in DRAM. The replaceable system cartridge supplies at least {minimum_os_rom_bytes} bytes. EEPROM BIOS remains boot/diagnostic firmware; optional services, larger utilities and patches load from disk rather than copying the entire ROM into RAM.

Executable ABI versions select legacy adapters, stable library dispatch and capability discovery. Preserve documented ERA instruction semantics, C calling conventions and layouts, syscall entry/numbers, loading, errors and legacy signals. Privileged drivers, undocumented kernel assumptions and direct hardware access need separate qualification; Z80 C code must be recompiled. Versioned dispatch and page-sized RAM overlays patch code after ROM checksum/version checks, with recovery boot bypassing disk patches. A qualified minor revision can be installed by exchanging a host-compatible cartridge.

The preferred DRAM allocation is {preferred_dram_bytes} bytes; the 256 KiB minimum is an engineering fit target, not a measured guarantee, and the server retains its existing 1 MiB configuration. Illustrative allocations are 40 KiB for kernel state/tables/stacks, 24 KiB for filesystem buffers, 16 KiB for translation metadata, 12 KiB for terminal/UI input, 20 KiB for services/patch reserve and 144 KiB for applications. Shared ROM, sparse page tables, small kernel stacks and reliable copy-on-write reduce demand. Allocation failure must be handled; ROM cannot replace writable RAM. Later swap requires qualified restart, locking and I/O with fault handlers resident, and should address occasional pressure rather than routine oversizing.

A compact monolithic kernel timer-preempts user processes while bounding non-preemptible kernel critical sections. Priority aging, sleeping I/O and atomic sleep/wakeup provide fairness; short interrupts defer work. Validate user pointers, protect kernel/device mappings, constrain per-process memory/files/requests, bound driver retries and timeouts, and retain responsive administrative termination. Process exit cleans files, memory, locks and child state. Kernel-controlled DMA uses checked pinned buffers; process isolation alone protects neither kernel/driver faults nor DMA. A fully preemptible kernel and application threads are not initial requirements.

A versioned inode filesystem separates directory entries from metadata, using {allocation_block_bytes}-byte blocks and {block_identifier_bits}-bit block IDs. The initial qualification range is {qualification_volume_mb} MB, not a capacity ceiling or bundled-drive change. Direct/indirect pointers, metadata timestamps/link counts, bounded caches, mounts and logical-sector drivers with CHS translation support the layout.

Clean/dirty state, a consistency checker, ordered metadata writes, explicit synchronization and tested backup/restore establish recoverability. Exact disk format/limits, file-offset and timestamp representation, legacy import/mount behaviour and controller persistence guarantees remain open. A later small metadata journal still needs power-loss/write-order testing and does not alone ensure application-data durability.

Numeric users/groups, owner/group/other permissions including directory search, creation masks, real/effective credentials and login/home directories define access. Protect salted, costed password hashes within CPU budgets and enforce permissions on every relevant kernel operation. Device/mount/configuration administration and audit records are protected. Qualify credential/exec transitions before enabling set-user-ID programs; servers authenticate users rather than trusting supplied UIDs. Extended ACLs are later work.

The initial subset defines file/descriptor operations and errors; descriptor duplication/inheritance; copy-on-write fork, exec, wait, status and environment; signals/masks/dispositions and interruption; canonical/raw terminals and foreground process groups; hierarchical paths, working directories and hard/symbolic links; pipes, EOF/broken-pipe handling and readiness multiplexing; shell quoting, redirection, pipelines, variables and statuses; wall and monotonic clocks with explicit timestamp formats. Publish an implemented/partial/absent matrix and unsupported-operation errors rather than claiming conformance from names. Efficient spawn, broader file control/mapping, full job control/pseudo-terminals, sockets/IPC, utilities, locales, threads and timers are later additions.

Applications own business logic and semantic Open/Save/Select/Cancel commands. A shared abstraction provides events, menus, forms, lists, focus, layout, measurement and drawing contexts; translation adapters preserve TUI, terminal, device and legacy ABI behaviour above native process/file/IPC/timer/input/display services. These are logical library/service layers, not four mandatory processes or IPC hops.

A bounded event queue handles keys, timers, focus, redraw and future pointer events. Opaque view/window handles initially describe text regions; clipping, invalidation, repaint, layout constraints and text measurement use separate cell/pixel coordinates. Clipboard/selection ownership is bounded, and graphics/font/colour/pointer support is discovered by version and capability. Compact text state, dirty regions and redraw callbacks avoid a mandatory full-screen backing bitmap. A later GUI can host old character applications in terminal windows without automatically redesigning them.

Release tests must cover legacy binary regressions, fairness/termination under CPU load, injected faults and cleanup, concurrent disk/terminal/DMA I/O, power loss and durable saves, credentials/permissions, measured ROM/RAM use with Abacus/compiler/server workloads, and TUI fallback/legacy terminal behaviour.

This operating system targets native ERA/AIONix on {host_base_computer_athena} and {host_base_computer_athena_server}. The recorded installed-RAM requirement is {minimum_ram_kib} KiB. The software image is supplied in its matching physical ROM cartridge; hardware construction belongs to that cartridge. Application workspace and ROM footprint remain unspecified beyond the explicit system-ROM requirement.

chapters.description:
The system adapts {base_version} for banked-ROM execution while preserving standard entry points, loading conventions and available-memory boundaries. A single foreground application can use ordinary CP/M console/file services; richer behaviour uses the separate versioned Logix API.

The CCP interprets commands and loads disk/cartridge programs; BDOS supplies file services through the machine BIOS, which adapts calls to Logix drivers. Motherboard ROM supplies {firmware_contents}. The system cartridge supplies {cartridge_contents}; command buffers and mutable system state remain in RAM. ROM constants/code must be separated from state and self-modifying routines adapted.

In conventional CP/M, 0000H–00FFH holds vectors, default file-control data and the command/disk buffer. Programs load at {program_load_address} in the transient program area and call BDOS through {bdos_entry}; CCP, BDOS and BIOS occupy higher memory. The TPA is application RAM, not an OS module. Transient editor/copy/assembler/debugger/maintenance utilities load when needed.

Compared with 1.3, the 1.4 base supports four logical drives, BIOS sector translation and extra drive state; BDOS begins one 256-byte page lower while CCP/BIOS bases stay fixed. It revises disk errors, returns DE consistently with HL and splits BDOS into PL/M logic plus an assembly interface. Vanilla 1.4 does not contain Logix banked-ROM, cartridge, dynamic-driver, TUI/clipboard/workspace services or the later CP/M 2.0 disk-parameter-block model.

Logix boot firmware discovers cartridges and provides diagnostics/recovery. The common-memory runtime preserves accessible entry code, stack and interrupt state across nested bank switches, following {memory_model_id}. Drivers in motherboard/device ROM or extensions register video, keyboard, floppy and FlexiBUS services. BIOS and relevant BDOS assumptions must match Aurelia disk formats. DMA uses physical-bank descriptors, bounded transfers and ready handshakes; drain or abort it before warm boot or buffer reuse. Video uploads expose dedicated sprite SRAM and atomic descriptors with backpressure, falling back to programmed I/O where needed.

chapters.chapter_name: Shared TUI ownership and application behaviour
chapters.description:
The system owns {tui_contract_id}, exposed through {portable_api_id} and {display_api_id}. It supplies reusable controls, while {consumer_business_tools_aurelia}, {consumer_abacus_1}, {consumer_abacus_2}, {consumer_bpi_suite} and {consumer_pulse_1} retain their document, calculation, file-management and scheduling logic.

Screen services query usable dimensions, clip/scroll and distinguish document from display coordinates. Compact 40-column and expanded 80-column layouts fit dialogs, names and errors; semantic text/selection/warning roles map to colour or monochrome. Structured character, function/navigation and modifier events support blocking or polled input. Shared fields, lists, menus, forms, popups and focus movement use consistent editing and clipboard commands. Clipboard formats, lengths, capacity, ownership and errors are explicit. Contexts are created/destroyed and activated/deactivated with redraw; one may cover the whole screen. System timing and repeat replace CPU-speed loops.

Sequential applications can use these services without multitasking. Exact widgets, clipboard capacity and workspace reservations remain implementation choices. Preserve legacy console behaviour and stable target ABI, use capability discovery, and avoid hard-coded stride, video addresses, last columns or hardware registers. The same documented API spans Aurelia, Aurelia+ and Artemis; Artemis mediates shared display/clipboard access between processes.

This operating system targets Z80/CP/M on {host_base_computer_aurelia} and {host_base_computer_aurelia_plus}. The recorded installed-RAM requirement is {minimum_ram_kib} KiB. The software image is supplied in its matching physical ROM cartridge; hardware construction belongs to that cartridge. Application workspace and ROM footprint remain unspecified.

chapters.description: The suite is implemented in AION C around a relational base engine, the Logix TUI and native FlexiBUS printing. General Accounting covers ledger, simplified receivables/payables, payroll integration and balance sheets. Accounts Receivable tracks customers, open invoices, payments and statements; Accounts Payable tracks vendors, liabilities, cash-flow obligations and cheque printing. Inventory Control handles stock, purchase orders, movement journals and profitability. Payroll handles employee hours, local/federal withholding, benefits and payroll cheques.

Selected balances or monthly totals are exported as versioned delimited text with named columns, period, currency, account identifiers, decimal amounts and control totals. Close BPI before loading Abacus to use these as independent planning inputs; there is no automatic write-back, simultaneous execution or live database link. Reconcile counts/totals and test rounding, quoting, disk-full handling, memory and save/reopen; label prepared demonstration data.

The implementation uses {portable_api_id}. Keep application/document algorithms separate from platform adapters; query display dimensions and attributes, use semantic colours and clipping, and handle allocation failures with bounded buffers and banked-object handles. Persistent records are explicitly encoded and versioned rather than raw structures or pointers. Recompile and adapt OS-specific modules for another target, then test its resource limits; source portability does not extend the list of qualified hosts.

implementation_design.title: BPI transactional client/server v1
implementation_design.architecture: Thin Z80/ERA clients send bounded business operations to an Artemis PRO server. Query evaluation, indexes, validation, accounting posting and transactions execute on the server; clients do not fetch arbitrary database pages.

transactions.concurrency: Single serialized writer for v1 with short transactions and bounded reader locks; no long interactive transaction while a user edits a form.
transactions.commit: Append checked log records and a commit marker, force them to durable storage, then acknowledge. Apply/replay committed changes idempotently.
transactions.recovery: On startup validate checksums and recover committed log records; incomplete transactions never become visible. Use shadow page/index replacement or another explicitly validated torn-write-safe method.
transactions.failure: Do not claim durable commit until disk/controller completion semantics are proven; no battery-backed cache is assumed.
transactions.log_format: Redo-only changed-record/page after-images with transaction ID, sequence, length and checksum; the commit marker covers transaction record count and checksum. Persist duplicate-suppression outcomes in the same transaction.
transactions.buffer_policy: Do not write uncommitted changes to database files (no-steal); cap transaction size to available transaction buffers.
transactions.checkpoint: Write replacement pages and indexes to new locations, force them, then alternate checksummed generation-numbered root/checkpoint records. Retain the preceding valid root and necessary redo log until the new checkpoint is durable.

protocol.transport: Length-framed requests over TCP; bounded messages and chunked results.
protocol.duplicate_suppression: Store committed write request IDs and outcomes durably. After reconnect, clients query status or retry with the same ID; never post the same payment twice.

data_integrity: Amounts use explicitly scaled integers/decimal rules, never unspecified binary floating-point rounding.
Record currency, rounding, posting dates, account periods and unique document IDs.
Cross-module posting is atomic and produces an append-only audit record.
operations: Backup captures a consistent checkpoint plus required logs; test restoration onto a clean disk.
Bounded log growth, disk-full handling and operator-visible recovery status
Plan backups and report traffic around the negotiated shared 100/250/500/1000 kbit/s raw LAN budget and measured payload throughput; slower admitted hosts limit the whole network.

initial_limits.client_policy: Bounded pages of results and forms; no entire-table download or whole-document duplication.

acceptance_tests: Full disk, corrupt log tail and failed backup restore

distribution.network_operation: Start under the existing networking OS, connect to server, and load further modules/data over the network; bootstrap remains local.
distribution.data_access: Business transactions, validation and database writes remain server-side; clients do not directly modify shared database files.

chapters.description: This edition sends bounded business operations to the relational accounting service on {server_host_id} running {server_edition_id}. Queries, indexes, validation, posting and transactions stay server-side; clients receive bounded pages of forms/results rather than arbitrary database pages or whole tables. {network_stack_id} supplies the network path. Robustness and capacity remain acceptance targets.

Version 1 serializes writers with short transactions and bounded reader locks; editing a form must not hold an interactive transaction open. Redo after-images carry transaction ID, sequence, length and checksum; a commit marker covers record count and checksum. Force log and commit marker to durable storage before acknowledging, then apply/replay changes idempotently. Persist request IDs and outcomes in the same transaction so a lost acknowledgement can be retried without posting a payment twice.

Uncommitted data must not reach database files; transaction size is limited by buffers. Checkpoint into replacement pages/indexes, force them, then alternate checksummed generation-numbered roots. Retain the previous valid root and required redo log until the new checkpoint is durable. Startup validates checksums and exposes only committed work. Torn-write safety and disk/controller completion semantics must be proven; no battery-backed cache is assumed.

Length-framed TCP requests use {request_fields}. Operations are {operations}; messages and streamed results are bounded. Reconnecting clients query status or reuse the original durable request ID.

Amounts use explicit scaled-integer/decimal rules with currency, rounding, posting dates, periods and unique document IDs. Cross-module postings are atomic and append an audit record. Backups capture a consistent checkpoint and required logs, with restoration tested on a clean disk. Bound log growth, handle full disks and expose recovery status.

The server target is {server_ram_kib} KiB with {concurrent_sessions_target} concurrent sessions. Plan backups/reports around the negotiated shared 100/250/500/1000 kbit/s raw LAN budget and measured payload throughput; the slowest admitted host limits the common rate. Test power loss around acknowledgements, duplicate retries, concurrent postings, disk-full/corrupt-log failures, backup restoration and a 48 KiB Aurelia client.

The implementation uses {portable_api_id}. Keep application/document algorithms separate from platform adapters; query display dimensions and attributes, use semantic colours and clipping, and handle allocation failures with bounded buffers and banked-object handles. Persistent records are explicitly encoded and versioned rather than raw structures or pointers. Recompile and adapt OS-specific modules for another target, then test its resource limits; source portability does not extend the list of qualified hosts.

This client targets Z80/CP/M on {host_base_computer_aurelia} and {host_base_computer_aurelia_plus}. The recorded installed-RAM requirement is {minimum_ram_kib} KiB. It requires {runtime_cpm_aurelia_networking}. A local startup diskette boots the client under its existing networking OS before bounded transfers load further modules or data. This edition is supplied as part of its containing package. Application workspace and ROM footprint remain unspecified.

compatibility_policy.eligibility: Any manufacturer or independent integrator may implement the published environment without a bespoke partnership or mandatory certification.
compatibility_policy.binary: Existing Z80 binaries require compatible instruction execution and the specified OS/runtime and memory behaviour; CP/M alone is insufficient. Other processors need an appropriate port or execution solution.
compatibility_policy.hardware: Native video, keyboards, disks and printers may be exposed through adapters. FlexiBUS and Logix video hardware are separate optional profiles. Full hardware clones may implement those published interfaces under their applicable terms.
compatibility_policy.applications: Named supported platforms are tested configurations, not an exclusive permission list. Independently implemented environments may run properly licensed applications; certification identifies precisely what AION tested.
compatibility_policy.delivery: Printed manuals/source listings and disks; host/media conversion quoted separately.
compatibility_policy.certification: Optional, configuration- and version-specific. Manufacturer-declared compatibility is distinct from AION-tested application compatibility. FlexiBUS electrical/protocol and Logix display tests are separate claims.

chapters.description:

It supplies runtime-adapter source and redistribution terms, diagnostics and failure/resource-limit tests, plus Abacus/Business Tools workloads for calculation, interchange, printing and save/reopen. Manuals, source listings, machine-readable disks and versioned result forms support independent implementations.

Any manufacturer or integrator can implement the environment without a bespoke partnership or mandatory certification. Existing Z80 binaries need compatible instructions and OS/runtime/memory behaviour; CP/M alone is insufficient, and another processor needs a port or execution solution. Native video, keyboard, disk and printer interfaces may use adapters; FlexiBUS and Logix video are separate optional profiles, including applicable terms for hardware clones.

Named supported platforms are tested configurations, not an exclusive permission list for properly licensed applications. Optional certification applies to an exact configuration/version and distinguishes a manufacturer’s claim from AION-tested application compatibility; FlexiBUS electrical/protocol and Logix display claims are separate. Printed documentation/source listings accompany disks; host/media conversion is a separate delivery requirement.
This application suite targets Z80/CP/M. No specific host configuration is listed. The edition is delivered on diskette. Application workspace and ROM footprint remain unspecified.

Text channels, posts/replies, file/revision/commit links, calendars, meetings, invitations, tasks, owners, deadlines and milestones support collaboration.

Artemis supports local ERA/Z80 builds. Heavy or ERA work can be queued on the server; Aurelia/Aurelia+ retain local Z80 tools. Breakthru TUI adapters and separate target binaries, startup and libraries serve CP/M/Z80 and AIONix/ERA. Reproducible builds record source revision, compiler version, settings and target libraries. Apple and Commodore packages are future work, without launch or binary-compatibility claims.

The server baseline is Artemis PRO with 1 MiB recommended RAM. The existing 5 MB disk supports bounded pilots only; archive old history, rotate external floppy backups and qualify larger storage for substantial projects. It is not included in the software definition. Network transfers are bounded, saves acknowledged and workspaces recoverable after disconnect. Four concurrent developers is a validation target, not measured throughput. Gate release on commit recovery, access control, backup/restore, conflicts and both target regression suites.

Sponsored deployments must supply and qualify their own workstation/server capacity, storage, concurrency and dedicated support. This engineering requirement does not change retail entitlement.
